Coral NPU is an Open Source IP designed by Google Research and is freely available for integration into ultra-low-power System-on-Chips (SoCs) targeting wearable devices such as hearables, augmented reality (AR) glasses and smart watches.\n4\t\n5\tCoral NPU is a neural processing unit (NPU), also known as an AI accelerator or deep-learning processor. Coral NPU is based on the 32-bit RISC-V Instruction Set Architecture (ISA).\n6\t\n7\tCoral NPU includes three distinct processor components that work together: matrix, vector (SIMD), and scalar.\n8\t\n9\t![Coral NPU Archicture](doc/images/arch_data_flow.png)\n10\t[Coral NPU Architecture Datasheet](https://developers.google.com/coral/guides/hardware/datasheet)\n11\t\n12\t## Coral NPU Features\n13\tCoral NPU offers the following top-level feature set:\n14\t\n15\t* RV32IMF_Zve32x RISC-V instruction set (specifically `rv32imf_zve32x_zicsr_zifencei_zbb`)\n16\t* 32-bit address space for applications and operating system kernels\n17\t* Four-stage processor, in-order dispatch, out-of-order retire\n18\t* Four-way scalar, two-way vector dispatch\n19\t* 128-bit SIMD, 256-bit (future) pipeline\n20\t* 8 KB ITCM memory (tightly-coupled memory for instructions)\n21\t* 32 KB DTCM memory (tightly-coupled memory for data)\n22\t* Both memories are single-cycle-latency SRAM, more efficient than cache memory\n23\t* AXI4 bus interfaces, functioning as both manager and subordinate, to interact with external memory and allow external CPUs to configure Coral NPU\n24\t\n25\t## System The SystemVerilog can be generated with:\n12\t\n13\t``` bash\n14\tbazel build //hdl/chisel/src/coralnpu:core_mini_axi_cc_library_emit_verilog\n15\t```\n16\t\n17\t### Module interfaces\n18\t\n19\t![CoralNPU AXI](images/coralnpu_axi.svg)\n20\t\n21\tThe interfaces to CoralNPU are defined as follows:\n22\t\n23\t|   Signal Bundle  |                   Description                             |\n24\t| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |\n25\t|       clk        | The clock of the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.                     |\n26\t|      reset       | The active-low reset signal for the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.  |\n27\t|      s_axi       | An AXI4 slave interface that can be used to write TCMs or touch CoralNPU CSRs. |\n28\t|      m_axi       | An AXI4 master interface used by CoralNPU to read/write to memories/CSRs. |\n29\t|       irqn       | Active-low interrupt to the CoralNPU core. Can be triggered by peripherals or other host processor. |\n30\t|       wfi        | Active-high signal from the CoralNPU core, indicating that the core is waiting for an interrupt. While this is active, CoralNPU is clock-gated. |\n31\t|      debug       | Debug interface to monitor CoralNPU instructions execution. This interface is typically only used for simulation. |\n32\t|      halted      | Output interface informing if the Core is running or not. Can be ignored. |\n33\t|      fault       | Output interface to determine if the Core hit a fault. reset strategy -- to ensure proper reset behavior, ensure that the clock runs for a cycle with reset active, before enabling either the internal clock gate (via CSR) or gating externally.\n168\t\n169\t## Booting CoralNPU\n170\tA note first -- in these examples, CoralNPU is located in the overall system memory map at 0x70000000.\n171\t\n172\t1. The instruction memory of CoralNPU must be initialized.\n173\t```c\n174\tvolatile uint8_t* coralnpu_itcm = (uint8_t*)0x00000000L;\n175\tfor (int i = 0; i < coralnpu_binary_len; ++i) {\n176\t    coralnpu_itcm[i] = coralnpu_binary[i];\n177\t}\n178\t```\n179\t\n180\tIf something like a DMA engine is present in your system, that is probably a better option for initializing the ITCM.\n181\t\n182\t2. Program the start PC\n183\tIf your program is linked such that the starting address is 0, you may skip this.\n184\t\n185\t```c\n186\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_pc_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030004L;\n187\t*coralnpu_pc_csr = start_addr;\n188\t```\n189\t\n190\t3. Release clock gate\n191\t```c\n192\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;\n193\t*coralnpu_reset_csr = 1;\n194\t```\n195\t\n196\tAfter this, ensure you wait a cycle to allow CoralNPU's reset to occur.\n197\tIf you want to configure something like an interrupt that is connected to CoralNPU's\n198\tfault or halted outputs, this is a good time.\n199\t\n200\t4. Release reset\n201\t```c\n202\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;\n203\t*coralnpu_reset_csr = 0;\n204\t```\n205\t\n206\tAt this point, CoralNPU will begin executing at the PC programmed in step 2.\n207\t\n208\t5. Monitor for `io_halted`\n209\tThe status of CoralNPU's execution can be checked by reading the status CSR:\n210\t```c\n211\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_status_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030008L;\n212\tuint32_t status = *coralnpu_status_csr;\n213\tbool halted = status & 1;\n214\tbool fault = status & 2;\n215\t```\n216\t\n217\t# CoralNPU CSRs\n218\tNote: These are CSRs that are intended to be read or written externally\n219\tto CoralNPU, e.g. by the host processor in a system.\n220\tThey are not the same as the RISC-V CSRs accessed via the Zicsr ISA extension.\n221\t\n222\t### Register: `RESET_CONTROL`\n223\t*   **Offset**: `0x0`\n224\t*   **Description**: Controls reset and clock gating for the CoralNPU core. The design\n5\tof CoralNPU starts with domain and matrix capabilities; vector and scalar\n6\tcapabilities are then added for a fused design.\n7\t\n8\t## Block Diagram\n9\t\n10\t![CoralNPU block diagram](images/coralnpu_block.png)\n11\t\n12\t## Scalar Core\n13\t\n14\tA simple RISC-V scalar frontend drives the command queues of the ML+SIMD\n15\tbackend.\n16\t\n17\tCoralNPU utilizes a custom RISC-V frontend (rv32im) that runs the minimal set of\n18\tinstructions to support an executor run-to-completion model (eg. no OS, no\n19\tinterrupts), with all control tasks onloaded to the SMC . The C extension\n20\tencoding is reclaimed (as per the risc-v specification) to provide the necessary\n21\tencoding space for the SIMD registers (6b indices), and to allow flexible type\n22\tencodings and instruction compression (stripmining) for the SIMD instruction\n23\tset. The scalar core is an in order machine with no speculation.\n24\t\n25\tThe branch policy in the fetch stage is backwards branches are taken and forward\n26\tbranches are not-taken, incurring a penalty cycle if the execute result does not\n27\tmatch the decision in the fetch unit.\n28\t\n29\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n30\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n31\tScalar (31)      | zero, x1..x31 | 32 bits\n32\tControl & Status | CSRx          | Various\n33\t\n34\t## Vector Core\n35\t\n36\tWe use SIMD and vector interchangeably, referring to a simple and practical SIMD\n37\tinstruction definition devoid of variable length behaviors. The scalar frontend\n38\tis decoupled from the backend by a FIFO structure that buffers vector\n39\tinstructions, posting only to the relevant command queues when dependencies are\n40\tresolved in the vector regfile. The vector core supports data widths of 8, 16, and 32 bits.\n41\t\n42\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n43\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n44\tVector (64)      | v0..v63       | 256 bits (eg. int32 x8)\n45\tAccumulator      | acc<8><8>     | 8x8x 32 bits\n46\t\n47\t\n48\t### MAC\n49\t\n50\tThe central component of the design is a quantized outer product\n51\tmultiply-accumulate engine. An outer-product engine provides two-dimensional\n52\tbroadcast structures to maximize the amount of deliverable compute with respect\n53\tto memory accesses. On one axis is a parallel broadcast (“wide”, convolution\n54\tweights), and the other axis the transpose shifted inputs of a number of batches\n55\t(“narrow”, eg. MobileNet XY batching).\n56\t\n57\t![CoralNPU MAC](images/coralnpu_aconv.png)\n58\t\n59\tThe outer-product construction is a vertical arrangement of multiple VDOT\n60\topcodes which utilize 4x 8bit multiplies reduced into 32 bit accumulators and\n61\tperforming 256 MACs per cycle.\n62\t\n63\t### Stripmining\n64\t\n65\tStrip mining is defined as folding array-based parallelism to fit the available\n66\thardware parallelism. To reduce frontend instruction dispatch pressure becoming\n67\ta bottleneck, and to natively support instruction level tiling patterns through\n68\tthe SIMD registers, the instruction encoding shall explicitly include a\n69\tstripmine mechanism that converts a single frontend dispatch event to the\n70\tcommand queue into four serialized issue events into the SIMD units. For\n71\tinstance a “vadd v0” in Dispatch will produce “vadd v0 : vadd v1 : vadd v2 :\n72\tvadd v3” at Issue. These will be processed as four discrete events.\n73\t\n74\t## Cache\n75\t\n76\tCaches exists as a single layer between the core and the first level of shared\n77\tSRAM. The L1 cache and scalar core frontend are an overhead to the rest of the\n78\tbackend compute pipeline and ideally are as small as possible.\n79\t\n80\tThe L1Icache is 8KB (256b blocks * 256 slots) with 4-way set associativity.\n81\t\n82\tThe L1Dcache sizing is towards the scalar core requirements to perform loop\n83\tmanagement and address generation. The L1Dcache is 16KB (SIMD256b) with low set\n84\tassociativity of 4-way. The L1Dcache is implemented with a dual bank\n85\tarchitecture where each bank is 8KB (similar to L1Icache). This property allows\n86\tfor a degree of next line prefetch. The L1Dcache also serves as an alignment\n87\tbuffer for the scalar and SIMD instructions to assist development and to\n88\tsimplify software support. In an embedded setting, the L1Dcache provides half of\n89\tthe memory bandwidth to the ML outer-product engine when only a single external\n90\tmemory port is provided. Line and all entry flushing is supported where the core\n91\tstalls until completion to simplify the contract.\n92\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. ROOT-LEVEL DOCUMENTATION\n\n### README.md\n- **Overview**: Coral NPU is an open-source neural processing unit based on 32-bit RISC-V ISA\n- **Architecture**: Three distinct processor components: matrix, vector (SIMD), and scalar\n- **Key Features**:\n  - RV32IMF_Zve32x RISC-V instruction set\n  - 32-bit address space\n  - Four-stage processor with in-order dispatch, out-of-order retire\n  - 8 KB ITCM + 32 KB DTCM (tightly-coupled SRAM)\n  - AXI4 bus interfaces (both manager and subordinate)\n- **System Requirements**: Bazel 7.4.1, Python 3.9-3.12, SRecord\n\n### doc/overview.md\n- **Block Diagram**: Shows core structure with scalar, vector, and ML components\n- **Scalar Core**: Custom RISC-V frontend (rv32im), runs minimal instruction set for run-to-completion model (no OS, no interrupts)\n- **Vector Core**: SIMD with registers v0..v63 (256 bits), MAC engine with outer-product design, stripmining support\n- **Cache**: L1Icache (8KB, 256b blocks), L1Dcache (16KB dual-bank)\n\n### doc/integration_guide.md\n- **AXI Integration**: Complete module interface specification\n- **CSR Interface**: RESET_CONTROL, PC_START, STATUS registers at memory map 0x30000\n- **Booting Sequence**: Initialize ITCM → Program start PC → Release clock gate → Release reset → Monitor halted/fault\n- **Memory Map**: ITCM (0x0000-0x1FFF), DTCM (0x10000-0x17FFF), CSR (0x30000+)\n\n### doc/simulation.md\n- Describes VCS simulator support with environment variable configuration\n\n### CONTRIBUTING.md\n- Open Source Community Guidelines\n- Contributor License Agreement required (Google CLA)\n- Gerrit code review process\n\n---\n\n## 2. RULES DIRECTORY (Build System)\n\n### rules/chisel.bzl\n- **Purpose**: Build rules for Chisel HDL generation\n- **Key Functions**:\n  - `chisel_library()`: Wrapper for scala_library with Chisel plugins, macro annotations\n  - `chisel_binary()`: For Chisel main classes\n  - `chisel_test()`: Runs Scala tests, includes both scalatest and sh_test wrapper\n  - `chisel_cc_library()`: Generates Verilog from Chisel, creates verilator_cc_library and SystemC versions\n- **Compilation Options**: \"-Ymacro-annotations\", \"-Xfatal-warnings\", explaintypes, feature, reflectiveCalls\n\n### rules/coco_tb.bzl\n- **Purpose**: Cocotb test framework integration with Verilator\n- **Key Functions**:\n  - `verilator_cocotb_model`: Builds Verilator model with DPI/C++ dependencies\n  - `verilator_cocotb_test()`: Wrapper for cocotb tests with Verilator\n  - `vcs_cocotb_test()`: VCS simulator variant\n  - `cocotb_test_suite()`: Runs tests across multiple simulators\n- **Resource Management**: CPU reservation per Verilator action (min 4 cores, based on MAKE_JOBS)\n- **Parallelism**: Dynamic scheduling based on host CPU count\n\n### rules/coralnpu_v2.bzl\n- **Purpose**: Build rules for CoralNPU software binaries\n- **Key Macro**: `coralnpu_v2_binary()` - Creates RISC-V ELF, BIN, and VMEM files\n- **Features**:\n  - Custom linker script generation with memory size parameters\n  - ITCM/DTCM size configuration\n  - Stack/heap configuration\n  - Semihosting support option\n  - Generates .elf, .bin, .vmem output groups\n- **Toolchain**: Uses `//toolchain/crt` or `//toolchain/crt:crt_semihosting`\n\n### Other Key Rules Files\n- **autogen.bzl**: SCM info generation\n- **verilog.bzl**: Verilog library handling\n- **lint.bzl**: Verilator linting rules (vcstatic_lint)\n- **utils.bzl**: Template rules, cc_embed_data\n- **linker.bzl**: Linker script generation\n- **mpact.bzl**: MPACT simulator bindings\n\n---\n\n## 3. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01C9RyKGaRHbmSixzYwE8hoS","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# CoralNPU\n2\t\n3\tCoralNPU is a RISCV CPU built with custom SIMD instructions and microarchitectural\n4\tdecisions that align with the dataplane properties of an ML accelerator. The design\n5\tof CoralNPU starts with domain and matrix capabilities; vector and scalar\n6\tcapabilities are then added for a fused design.\n7\t\n8\t## Block Diagram\n9\t\n10\t![CoralNPU block diagram](images/coralnpu_block.png)\n11\t\n12\t## Scalar Core\n13\t\n14\tA simple RISC-V scalar frontend drives the command queues of the ML+SIMD\n15\tbackend.\n16\t\n17\tCoralNPU utilizes a custom RISC-V frontend (rv32im) that runs the minimal set of\n18\tinstructions to support an executor run-to-completion model (eg. no OS, no\n19\tinterrupts), with all control tasks onloaded to the SMC . The C extension\n20\tencoding is reclaimed (as per the risc-v specification) to provide the necessary\n21\tencoding space for the SIMD registers (6b indices), and to allow flexible type\n22\tencodings and instruction compression (stripmining) for the SIMD instruction\n23\tset. The scalar core is an in order machine with no speculation.\n24\t\n25\tThe branch policy in the fetch stage is backwards branches are taken and forward\n26\tbranches are not-taken, incurring a penalty cycle if the execute result does not\n27\tmatch the decision in the fetch unit.\n28\t\n29\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n30\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n31\tScalar (31)      | zero, x1..x31 | 32 bits\n32\tControl & Status | CSRx          | Various\n33\t\n34\t## Vector Core\n35\t\n36\tWe use SIMD and vector interchangeably, referring to a simple and practical SIMD\n37\tinstruction definition devoid of variable length behaviors. The scalar frontend\n38\tis decoupled from the backend by a FIFO structure that buffers vector\n39\tinstructions, posting only to the relevant command queues when dependencies are\n40\tresolved in the vector regfile. The vector core supports data widths of 8, 16, and 32 bits.\n41\t\n42\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n43\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n44\tVector (64)      | v0..v63       | 256 bits (eg. int32 x8)\n45\tAccumulator      | acc<8><8>     | 8x8x 32 bits\n46\t\n47\t\n48\t### MAC\n49\t\n50\tThe central component of the design is a quantized outer product\n51\tmultiply-accumulate engine. An outer-product engine provides two-dimensional\n52\tbroadcast structures to maximize the amount of deliverable compute with respect\n53\tto memory accesses. On one axis is a parallel broadcast (“wide”, convolution\n54\tweights), and the other axis the transpose shifted inputs of a number of batches\n55\t(“narrow”, eg. MobileNet XY batching).\n56\t\n57\t![CoralNPU MAC](images/coralnpu_aconv.png)\n58\t\n59\tThe outer-product construction is a vertical arrangement of multiple VDOT\n60\topcodes which utilize 4x 8bit multiplies reduced into 32 bit accumulators and\n61\tperforming 256 MACs per cycle.\n62\t\n63\t### Stripmining\n64\t\n65\tStrip mining is defined as folding array-based parallelism to fit the available\n66\thardware parallelism. To reduce frontend instruction dispatch pressure becoming\n67\ta bottleneck, and to natively support instruction level tiling patterns through\n68\tthe SIMD registers, the instruction encoding shall explicitly include a\n69\tstripmine mechanism that converts a single frontend dispatch event to the\n70\tcommand queue into four serialized issue events into the SIMD units. For\n71\tinstance a “vadd v0” in Dispatch will produce “vadd v0 : vadd v1 : vadd v2 :\n72\tvadd v3” at Issue. These will be processed as four discrete events.\n73\t\n74\t## Cache\n75\t\n76\tCaches exists as a single layer between the core and the first level of shared\n77\tSRAM. The L1 cache and scalar core frontend are an overhead to the rest of the\n78\tbackend compute pipeline and ideally are as small as possible.\n79\t\n80\tThe L1Icache is 8KB (256b blocks * 256 slots) with 4-way set associativity.\n81\t\n82\tThe L1Dcache sizing is towards the scalar core requirements to perform loop\n83\tmanagement and address generation. The L1Dcache is 16KB (SIMD256b) with low set\n84\tassociativity of 4-way. The L1Dcache is implemented with a dual bank\n85\tarchitecture where each bank is 8KB (similar to L1Icache). This property allows\n86\tfor a degree of next line prefetch. The L1Dcache also serves as an alignment\n87\tbuffer for the scalar and SIMD instructions to assist development and to\n88\tsimplify software support. In an embedded setting, the L1Dcache provides half of\n89\tthe memory bandwidth to the ML outer-product engine when only a single external\n90\tmemory port is provided. Line and all entry flushing is supported where the core\n91\tstalls until completion to simplify the contract.\n92\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. reset strategy -- to ensure proper reset behavior, ensure that the clock runs for a cycle with reset active, before enabling either the internal clock gate (via CSR) or gating externally.\n168\t\n169\t## Booting CoralNPU\n170\tA note first -- in these examples, CoralNPU is located in the overall system memory map at 0x70000000.\n171\t\n172\t1. The instruction memory of CoralNPU must be initialized.\n173\t```c\n174\tvolatile uint8_t* coralnpu_itcm = (uint8_t*)0x00000000L;\n175\tfor (int i = 0; i < coralnpu_binary_len; ++i) {\n176\t    coralnpu_itcm[i] = coralnpu_binary[i];\n177\t}\n178\t```\n179\t\n180\tIf something like a DMA engine is present in your system, that is probably a better option for initializing the ITCM.\n181\t\n182\t2. Program the start PC\n183\tIf your program is linked such that the starting address is 0, you may skip this.\n184\t\n185\t```c\n186\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_pc_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030004L;\n187\t*coralnpu_pc_csr = start_addr;\n188\t```\n189\t\n190\t3. Release clock gate\n191\t```c\n192\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;\n193\t*coralnpu_reset_csr = 1;\n194\t```\n195\t\n196\tAfter this, ensure you wait a cycle to allow CoralNPU's reset to occur.\n197\tIf you want to configure something like an interrupt that is connected to CoralNPU's\n198\tfault or halted outputs, this is a good time.\n199\t\n200\t4. Release reset\n201\t```c\n202\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;\n203\t*coralnpu_reset_csr = 0;\n204\t```\n205\t\n206\tAt this point, CoralNPU will begin executing at the PC programmed in step 2.\n207\t\n208\t5. Monitor for `io_halted`\n209\tThe status of CoralNPU's execution can be checked by reading the status CSR:\n210\t```c\n211\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_status_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030008L;\n212\tuint32_t status = *coralnpu_status_csr;\n213\tbool halted = status & 1;\n214\tbool fault = status & 2;\n215\t```\n216\t\n217\t# CoralNPU CSRs\n218\tNote: These are CSRs that are intended to be read or written externally\n219\tto CoralNPU, e.g. by the host processor in a system.\n220\tThey are not the same as the RISC-V CSRs accessed via the Zicsr ISA extension.\n221\t\n222\t### Register: `RESET_CONTROL`\n223\t*   **Offset**: `0x0`\n224\t*   **Description**: Controls reset and clock gating for the CoralNPU core. On power-up, the core is held in reset with its clock gated. Functionally,\n6\tit's purpose is to translate memory instructions into transactions on the\n7\tappropriate subsystem.\n8\t\n9\t## Slots\n10\t\n11\tThe CoralNPU LSU uses a concept called _slots_ to handle memory transactions. A\n12\tslot is a data structure which manages the state of a single dispatched LSU\n13\toperation and determines what memory transaction should be performed. At its\n14\tcore, there exists a table in each slot which tracks which part of the memory\n15\toperation has been completed.\n16\t\n17\tFor example, below is the slot table for a word-store into address 0xDEADBEEF:\n18\t\n19\t| Index | Active |   Address  | Data |\n20\t| ----- | ------ | ---------- | ---- |\n21\t|   0   |    1   | 0xDEADBEEF | 0x01 |\n22\t|   1   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF0 | 0x23 |\n23\t|   2   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF1 | 0x45 |\n24\t|   3   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF2 | 0x67 |\n25\t|   4   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |\n26\t...\n27\t|   n   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |\n28\t\n29\tMemory transactions over TCM or AXI busses will read/write data in the slot\n30\ttable and flip the active bits to 0 as they are made.\n31\t\n32\tThe typical lifetime of a slot is as follows:\n33\t\n34\t1) **Idle**: An idle slot will dequeue a LsuOperation from the command queue.\n35\tScalar operations will move directly into **Transfer Memory** while vector\n36\toperations will go to the **Vector Update** state.\n37\t2) **Vector Update**: For vector operations masks, addresses (for indexed ops)\n38\tand data (for store ops) need to be received from the RvvCore. This stage is\n39\tbypassed for scalar operations.\n40\t3) **Transfer Memory**: While there are still active entries in the slot table,\n41\tthe active entry with the lowest \"index\" will be selected for a memory\n42\ttransaction. A scatter/gather unit will then select all other active entries\n43\t(although not necessarily contiguous) that will be bundled with the transaction.\n44\tThe appropriate memory bus (ibus, dbus, ebus) will then be selected and a memory\n45\ttransaction will be conducted. When there are no active entries, the slot moves\n46\tinto the next state (**Writeback**).\n47\t4) **Writeback**: Once all memory transactions are completed, the result must\n48\tbe written back to register files. Additionally, vector stores are\n49\t\"acknowledged\" back to the RvvCore. Scalar and floating point scores bypass this\n50\tstage. Once writeback is completed, the slot moves back into the\n51\t**Vector Update** state for LMUL > 1, or the **Idle** state.\n52\t\n53\tCoralNPU currently uses one \"slot\" in the LSU. In the future, multiple slots maybe\n54\tadded to allow multiple operations to partake in the same transaction.\n55\t\n56\t## Interfaces\n57\t\n58\t### LSU Command Interface\n59\t\n60\tThe LSU has a command interface coming from the dispatch unit and register file.\n61\t\n62\t| Signal Name   | Type          | Description                                                   |\n63\t| ------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |\n64\t| req.valid     | Bool          | If the LSU command is valid.                                  |\n65\t| req.op        |               | The LSU operation to execute.                                 |\n66\t| req.addr      | UInt(5)       | The RegFile address to write the result to for loads.         |\n67\t| req.pc        | UInt(32)      | The PC of the LSU instruction. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |\n45\t\n46\t### Timing/Pipeline\n47\t\n48\tThe MLU is a three stage pipeline, with the following stages:\n49\t\n50\t1. **Dispatch:** The dispatch unit determines if MLU operations can be executed.\n51\tAmongst the four lanes, the MLU accepts the first valid MLU instruction. This\n52\trequest will be processed next cycle.\n53\t2. **Compute:** The second stage performs computation of the multiplication,\n54\tusing the register read data from rs1 and rs2.\n55\t2. **Writeback:** The multiplication result is stored back to the register file.\n56\t\n57\tA waveform showing a typical interaction with the waveform can be found in\n58\tFigure 2:\n59\t\n60\t![image](../images/mlu_waveform.png)\n61\t\n62\tFigure 2: Mlu waveform.\n63\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. Our linker script will allocate them in DTCM and we'll query their\n61\tlocations in our test bench.\n62\t\n63\t### Defining Computation\n64\t\n65\tAs a simple example, let's add element-wise the elements from `input1_buffer`\n66\tto `input2_buffer`:\n67\t\n68\t```c++\n69\tuint32_t input1_buffer[8] __attribute__((section(\".data\")));\n70\tuint32_t input2_buffer[8] __attribute__((section(\".data\")));\n71\tuint32_t output_buffer[8] __attribute__((section(\".data\")));\n72\t\n73\tint main(int argc, char** argv) {\n74\t  for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {\n75\t    output_buffer[i] = input1_buffer[i] + input2_buffer[i];\n76\t  }\n77\t  return 0;\n78\t}\n79\t```\n80\t\n81\tThe core will halt when returning from `main`.\n82\t\n83\t### Compiling the program\n84\t\n85\tRun `bazel build tests/cocotb/tutorial:coralnpu_v2_program`\n86\tto generate `coralnpu_v2_program.elf`.\n87\t\n88\t## Creating the test bench\n89\t\n90\tOpen up [`tests/cocotb/tutorial/tutorial.py`](../../tests/cocotb/tutorial/tutorial.py)\n91\twhich contains the skeleton testbench:\n92\t\n93\t```python\n94\t@cocotb.test()\n95\tasync def core_mini_axi_tutorial(dut):\n96\t    \"\"\"Testbench to run your CoralNPU program.\"\"\"\n97\t    # Test bench setup\n98\t    core_mini_axi = CoreMiniAxiInterface(dut)\n99\t    await core_mini_axi.init()\n100\t    await core_mini_axi.reset()\n101\t    cocotb.start_soon(core_mini_axi.clock.start())\n102\t```\n103\t\n104\tFirst, we need to program ITCM with your program. The\n4\tfollowing describes the general rules we use to determine which instructions can\n5\tbe dispatcted.\n6\t\n7\t## In-order\n8\t\n9\tCoralNPU is an in-order core. This\n15\tprevents RAW and WAW data hazards. All execution units read their operands from\n16\tthe register file the cycle after the instructions are dispatched. While\n22\tthere are enough Alu and Bru units to service each lane, CoralNPU contains only\n23\t1 Mlu. SPI\n168\t    * clock is toggled as a Bool input at a 10:13 ratio to approximate truly async clocks.\n169\t    */\n170\t  def withDualClock(body: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper => Unit): Unit = {\n171\t    simulate(new Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) { dut =>\n172\t      // Reset — toggle SPI clock during reset so system-reset-only\n173\t      // CDC FIFOs (clocked by spi_clk) see the reset posedge.\n174\t      dut.reset.poke(true.B)\n175\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(true.B)\n176\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n177\t      dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n178\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(false.B)\n179\t      for (_ <- 0 until 5) {\n180\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(true.B)\n181\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n182\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n183\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n184\t      }\n185\t      dut.reset.poke(false.B)\n186\t      dut.clock.step(5)\n187\t\n188\t      body(dut)\n189\t    }\n190\t  }\n191\t\n192\t  /** Dual-clock tick state — tracks when to toggle SPI clock relative to sys clock. */\n193\t  class DualClockState(dut: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) {\n194\t    var sysTime: Long     = 0\n195\t    var nextSysEdge: Long = SYS_HALF\n196\t    var nextSpiEdge: Long = SPI_HALF\n197\t    var spiLevel: Boolean = false\n198\t\n199\t    /** Advance one sim time unit, toggling whichever clock(s) fire. Returns 's', 'p', or 'b'. */\n200\t    def tick(): Char = {\n201\t      if (nextSysEdge < nextSpiEdge) {\n202\t        sysTime = nextSysEdge\n203\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n204\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n205\t        's'\n206\t      } else if (nextSpiEdge < nextSysEdge) {\n207\t        sysTime = nextSpiEdge\n208\t        spiLevel = !spiLevel\n209\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n210\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n211\t        // Don't step sys clock — just toggle SPI\n212\t        // But we need at least one eval to propagate. spiLevel = !spiLevel\n219\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n220\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n221\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n222\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n223\t        'b'\n224\t      }\n225\t    }\n226\t\n227\t    /** Advance until n SPI posedges have occurred. */\n228\t    def spiCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n229\t      var count = 0\n230\t      while (count < n) {\n231\t        val w = tick()\n232\t        if ((w == 'p' || w == 'b') && spiLevel) count += 1\n233\t      }\n234\t    }\n235\t\n236\t    /** Advance until n sys posedges have occurred. */\n237\t    def bothCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n238\t      var count = 0\n239\t      while (count < n) {\n240\t        val w = tick()\n241\t        if (w == 's' || w == 'b') count += 1\n242\t      }\n243\t    }\n244\t\n245\t    // SPI protocol helpers\n246\t\n247\t    def spiXferByte(tx: Int): Unit = {\n248\t      for (bit <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n249\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke((((tx >> bit) & 1) != 0).B)\n250\t        spiCycles(1)\n251\t      }\n252\t    }\n253\t\n254\t    def spiRecvByte(): Int = {\n255\t      var rx = 0\n256\t      for (_ <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n257\t def csbAssert(): Unit = {\n265\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(false.B)\n266\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n267\t    }\n268\t\n269\t    def csbDeassert(): Unit = {\n270\t 0xff)\n280\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 24) & 0xff).toInt)\n281\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 16) & 0xff).toInt)\n282\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 8) & 0xff).toInt)\n283\t      spiXferByte((addr & addr(32), mask(16), data(128), user(23))\n69\t  // V2 TL-D is 162 bits: Cat(opcode(3), param(3), size(4), source(8),\n70\t  //   sink(1), data(128), user(14), error(1))\n71\t  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------\n72\t  val TL_GET             = 4.U(3.W)\n73\t  val TL_ACCESS_ACK      = 0.U(3.W)\n74\t  val TL_ACCESS_ACK_DATA = 1.U(3.W)\n75\t\n76\t  val respPending = RegInit(false.B)\n77\t  val respReq     = RegInit(0.U.asTypeOf(new OpenTitanTileLink.A_Channel(tlul_p)))\n78\t  val tlAReady    = RegInit(true.B)\n79\t\n80\t  v2.io.q_tl_a.ready := tlAReady\n81\t\n82\t  val aValid = v2.io.q_tl_a.valid\n83\t  val aData  = v2.io.q_tl_a.bits\n84\t\n85\t  // Single-driver style: accept A → latch + deassert ready; D handshake → false.B, respPending))\n90\t  respReq     := Mux(acceptA, aData, respReq)\n91\t  tlAReady    := Mux(acceptA, false.B, Mux(completeD, true.B, tlAReady))\n92\t\n93\t  // Decode latched request (217-bit positions)\n94\t  val reqOpcode = respReq.opcode\n95\t  val reqParam  = respReq.param\n96\t  val reqSize   = respReq.size\n97\t  val reqSource = respReq.source\n98\t  val reqAddr   = respReq.address\n99\t\n100\t  val respOpcode =\n101\t    Mux(reqOpcode === TLULOpcodesA.Get.asUInt, TLULOpcodesD.AccessAckData, TLULOpcodesD.AccessAck)\n102\t  val respData = Cat(0.U(96.W), reqAddr)\n103\t\n104\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.valid       := respPending\n105\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.opcode := respOpcode.asUInt\n106\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.param  := 0.U(3.W)\n107\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.size   := reqSize\n108\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.source := reqSource\n109\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.sink   := 0.U(1.W)\n110\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.data   := respData\n111\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.user   := 0.U.asTypeOf(new OpenTitanTileLink_D_User)\n112\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.error  := 0.U(1.W)\n113\t\n114\t  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------\n115\t  // TL-A capture registers (latch on A-channel handshake)\n116\t  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------\n117\t  val aHandshake = aValid && tlAReady\n118\t  val captured   = RegInit(false.B)\n119\t  val capOpcode  = RegInit(0.U(3.W))\n120\t  val capAddress = RegInit(0.U(32.W))\n121\t  val capData    = RegInit(0.U(128.W))\n122\t  val capCount   = RegInit(0.U(32.W))\n123\t\n124\t  // First-beat capture: latched on the first handshake after count was last\n125\t  // snapshot by the test (i.e., the first beat of each multi-beat burst).\n126\t  val firstCapAddress = RegInit(0.U(32.W))\n127\t  val firstCapData    = RegInit(0.U(128.W))\n128\t  val firstCapDone    = RegInit(false.B)\n129\t\n130\t  captured   := Mux(aHandshake, true.B, captured)\n131\t  capOpcode  := Mux(aHandshake, aData.opcode, capOpcode)\n132\t  capAddress := Mux(aHandshake, aData.address, capAddress)\n133\t  capData    := Mux(aHandshake, aData.data, capData)\n134\t  capCount   := Mux(aHandshake, capCount + 1.U, capCount)\n135\t\n136\t  when(io.tl_a_first_reset) {\n137\t    firstCapDone    := false.B\n138\t    firstCapAddress := 0.U\n139\t    firstCapData    := 0.U\n140\t  }.elsewhen(aHandshake && !firstCapDone) {\n141\t    firstCapAddress := aData.address\n142\t    firstCapData    := aData.data\n143\t    firstCapDone    := true.B\n144\t  }\n145\t\n146\t  io.tl_a_captured      := captured\n147\t  io.tl_a_cap_opcode    := capOpcode\n148\t  io.tl_a_cap_address   := capAddress\n149\t  io.tl_a_cap_data      := capData\n150\t  io.tl_a_cap_count     := capCount\n151\t  io.tl_a_first_address := firstCapAddress\n152\t  io.tl_a_first_data    := firstCapData\n153\t}\n154\t\n155\t// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n156\t// Test suite — ports all 6 C++ tests\n157\t// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n158\t\n159\tclass Spi2TLULV2Spec extends AnyFreeSpec with ChiselSim {\n160\t\n161\t  // Sys clock period = 10 units (SYS_HALF=5), SPI period = 13 units (SPI_HALF=6.5).\n162\t  // We use integer ratio: SYS_HALF=10, SPI_HALF=13.\n163\t  // Each clock.step(1) is one \"sim unit\". SPI toggles when the phase counter says so.\n164\t  val SYS_HALF = 10\n165\t  val SPI_HALF = 13\n166\t\n167\t  /** Run the simulation with dual-clock stepping. The main clock.step() drives the sys domain. SPI\n168\t    * clock is toggled as a Bool input at a 10:13 ratio to approximate truly async clocks.\n169\t    */\n170\t  def withDualClock(body: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper => Unit): Unit = {\n171\t    simulate(new Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) { dut =>\n172\t      // Reset — toggle SPI clock during reset so system-reset-only\n173\t      // CDC FIFOs (clocked by spi_clk) see the reset posedge.\n174\t      dut.reset.poke(true.B)\n175\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(true.B)\n176\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n177\t      dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n178\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(false.B)\n179\t      for (_ <- 0 until 5) {\n180\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(true.B)\n181\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n182\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n183\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n184\t      }\n185\t      dut.reset.poke(false.B)\n186\t      dut.clock.step(5)\n187\t\n188\t      body(dut)\n189\t    }\n190\t  }\n191\t\n192\t  /** Dual-clock tick state — tracks when to toggle SPI clock relative to sys clock. */\n193\t  class DualClockState(dut: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) {\n194\t    var sysTime: Long     = 0\n195\t    var nextSysEdge: Long = SYS_HALF\n196\t    var nextSpiEdge: Long = SPI_HALF\n197\t    var spiLevel: Boolean = false\n198\t\n199\t    /** Advance one sim time unit, toggling whichever clock(s) fire. Returns 's', 'p', or 'b'. */\n200\t    def tick(): Char = {\n201\t      if (nextSysEdge < nextSpiEdge) {\n202\t        sysTime = nextSysEdge\n203\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n204\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n205\t        's'\n206\t      } else if (nextSpiEdge < nextSysEdge) {\n207\t        sysTime = nextSpiEdge\n208\t        spiLevel = !spiLevel\n209\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n210\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n211\t        // Don't step sys clock — just toggle SPI\n212\t        // But we need at least one eval to propagate. Step sys clock to advance simulation.\n213\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n214\t        'p'\n215\t      } else {\n216\t        // Both edges coincide\n217\t        sysTime = nextSysEdge\n218\t        spiLevel = !spiLevel\n219\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n220\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n221\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n222\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n223\t        'b'\n224\t      }\n225\t    }\n226\t\n227\t    /** Advance until n SPI posedges have occurred. */\n228\t    def spiCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n229\t      var count = 0\n230\t      while (count < n) {\n231\t        val w = tick()\n232\t        if ((w == 'p' || w == 'b') && spiLevel) count += 1\n233\t      }\n234\t    }\n235\t\n236\t    /** Advance until n sys posedges have occurred. */\n237\t    def bothCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n238\t      var count = 0\n239\t      while (count < n) {\n240\t        val w = tick()\n241\t        if (w == 's' || w == 'b') count += 1\n242\t      }\n243\t    }\n244\t\n245\t    // SPI protocol helpers\n246\t\n247\t    def spiXferByte(tx: Int): Unit = {\n248\t      for (bit <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n249\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke((((tx >> bit) & 1) != 0).B)\n250\t        spiCycles(1)\n251\t      }\n252\t    }\n253\t\n254\t    def spiRecvByte(): Int = {\n255\t      var rx = 0\n256\t      for (_ <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n257\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n258\t        spiCycles(1)\n259\t        rx = (rx << 1) | (if (dut.io.spi_miso.peek().litValue != 0) 1 else 0)\n260\t      }\n261\t      rx\n262\t    }\n263\t\n264\t    def csbAssert(): Unit = {\n265\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(false.B)\n266\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n267\t    }\n268\t\n269\t    def csbDeassert(): Unit = {\n270\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n271\t      // Let DmaEngine finish draining CDC FIFOs before CSB deasserts\n272\t      // (AsyncQueue safe mode coordinates reset on CSB deassert)\n273\t      bothCycles(500)\n274\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(true.B)\n275\t      bothCycles(50)\n276\t    }\n277\t\n278\t    def spiSendHeader(op: Int, addr: Long, len: Int): Unit = {\n279\t      spiXferByte(op & 0xff)\n280\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 24) & 0xff).toInt)\n281\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 16) & 0xff).toInt)\n282\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 8) & 0xff).toInt)\n283\t      spiXferByte((addr & 0xff).toInt)\n284\t      spiXferByte((len >> 8) & 0xff)\n285\t      spiXferByte(len & 0xff)\n286\t    }\n287\t\n288\t    /** Collect n raw MISO bits. Returns array of bytes packed MSB-first per byte. */\n289\t    def collectMisoBits(nbits: Int): Array[Int] = {\n290\t      val buf = new Array[Int]((nbits + 7) / 8)\n291\t      for (i <- 0 until nbits) {\n292\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n293\t        spiCycles(1)\n294\t        val byteIdx = i / 8\n295\t        val bitIdx  = 7 - (i % 8)\n296\t        if (dut.io.spi_miso.peek().litValue != 0) {\n297\t          buf(byteIdx) |= (1 << bitIdx)\n298\t        }\n299\t      }\n300\t      buf\n301\t    }\n302\t\n303\t    /** Wait for TL-A capture count to reach expected value. */\n304\t    def waitTlACapture(expectedCount: Long, timeoutSys: Int = 200): Boolean = {\n305\t      var sc = 0\n306\t      while (sc < timeoutSys) {\n307\t        val w = tick()\n308\t        if (w == 's' || w == 'b') {\n309\t          sc += 1\n310\t          if (dut.io.tl_a_cap_count.peek().litValue >= expectedCount) return true\n311\t        }\n312\t      }\n313\t      false\n314\t    }\n315\t\n316\t    /** Reset the first-beat capture registers so the next A-channel handshake is captured. */\n317\t    def resetFirstCapture(): Unit = {\n318\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(true.B)\n319\t      dut.clock.step(1)\n320\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(false.B)\n321\t    }\n322\t\n323\t    /** Send a multi-beat write frame: header(op=0x02, addr, len=numBeats-1) + numBeats*16 payload\n324\t      * bytes.\n325\t      */\n326\t    def spiWriteMulti(addr: Long, beats: Seq[Array[Int]]): Unit = {\n327\t      csbAssert()\n328\t      spiSendHeader(0x02, addr, beats.length - 1)\n329\t      for (beat <- beats; byte <- beat) spiXferByte(byte)\n330\t      csbDeassert()\n331\t    }\n332\t\n333\t  }\n334\t\n335\t  /** Search for a bit pattern (needle) in a bit buffer (haystack). Both are packed MSB-first per\n336\t    * byte. Returns bit offset or -1.\n337\t    */\n338\t  def findBitPattern(\n339\t      haystack: Array[Int],\n340\t      hayBits: Int,\n341\t      needle: Array[Int],\n342\t      needleBits: Int\n343\t  ): Int = {\n344\t    for (off <- 0 to (hayBits - needleBits)) {\n345\t      var matched = true\n346\t      var b       = 0\n347\t      while (b < needleBits && matched) {\n348\t        val hi     = off + b\n349\t        val hayBit = (haystack(hi / 8) >> (7 - (hi % 8))) & 1\n350\t        val ndlBit = (needle(b / 8) >> (7 - (b     % 8))) & 1\n351\t        if (hayBit != ndlBit) matched = false\n352\t        b += 1\n353\t      }\n354\t      if (matched) return off\n355\t    }\n356\t    -1\n357\t  }\n358\t\n359\t  // =========================================================================\n360\t  // produces n Valid outputs where valid elements are\n  * compacted to output positions 0, 1, 2, ... in input order.\n  *\n  * IO ports use UInt for bits to remain generic.\n  */\nclass AlignerIO(width: Int, n: Int) extends Bundle {\n  val in  = Input(Vec(n, new Bundle {\n    val valid = Bool()\n    val bits  = UInt(width.W)\n  }))\n  val out = Output(Vec(n, new Bundle {\n    val valid = Bool()\n    val bits  = UInt(width.W)\n  }))\n}\n\nclass Aligner[T <: Data](t: T, n: Int) extends Module {\n  val width = t.getWidth.max(1)\n\n  val io = IO(new Bundle {\n    val in  = Input(Vec(n, new Bundle {\n      val valid = Bool()\n      val bits  = UInt(width.W)\n    }))\n    val out = Output(Vec(n, new Bundle {\n      val valid = Bool()\n      val bits  = UInt(width.W)\n    }))\n  })\n\n  // For each output position o, we want the (o+1)-th valid input (0-indexed: the o-th valid input).\n  // We compute prefix sums of validity to find which input maps to each output.\n  for (o <- 0 until n) {\n    // Count valid inputs seen so far; `data` array of capacity entries stores available indices.\n  *   - `head` is the read pointer (next to allocate).\n  *   - `count` is the number of available (free) indices.\n  *   - Tail = (head + count) % capacity is the write pointer for freed indices.\n  *\n  * On reset: data[i] = i, head = 0, count = capacity.\n  * free.ready = (count < capacity) — there is room to accept a freed index.\n  *\n  * \"No pipe\" test: immediately after reset, count == capacity, so free.ready = false.\n  * \"Flow\" test: after allocating all, count == 0 and a freed index is available\n  *   combinationally (free.valid && free.ready => alloc.valid via bypass).\n  *\n  * The \"Flow\" test expects alloc.valid=true and alloc.bits=1 on the SAME cycle\n  * as free.valid is asserted (no clock edge). This means we need a combinational\n  * bypass: when count==0 and free fires, present the freed value directly on alloc.\n  */\nclass IndexAllocatorShifting(capacity: Int) extends IndexAllocator {\n  val indexW = log2Ceil(capacity + 1)\n\n  // Storage for free indices\n  val data  = Reg(Vec(capacity, UInt(indexW.W)))\n  val head  = RegInit(0.U(log2Ceil(capacity).W))\n  val count = RegInit(capacity.U(log2Ceil(capacity + 1).W))\n\n  // Initialise data to [0, 1, 2, ..., capacity-1]\n  for (i <- 0 until capacity) {\n    when (reset.asBool) {\n      data(i) := i.U\n    }\n  }\n\n  // Tail write pointer\n  val tail = ((head +& count) % capacity.U)(log2Ceil(capacity) - 1, 0)\n\n  // Combinational bypass: if count==0 and free is firing, present freed value immediately\n  val bypassActive = (count === 0.U) && io.free.valid\n\n  // alloc output\n  io.alloc.valid := (count > 0.U) || bypassActive\n  io.alloc.bits  := Mux(bypassActive, io.free.bits, data(head))\n\n  // free.ready: can accept a freed index when count < capacity AND not bypassing\n  // Also ready when count==0 and bypassing (the bypassed value goes straight out,\n  // so the freed slot is immediately consumed — no storage needed).\n  // But in the normal case: free.ready = count < capacity.\n  // \"No pipe\" test: at start count==capacity => free.ready=false. Correct.\n  // \"Flow\" test: after alloc all, count==0 < capacity => free.ready=true. Correct.\n  io.free.ready := count < capacity.U\n\n  // Update state on clock edge\n  val allocFire = io.alloc.valid && io.alloc.ready\n  val freeFire  = io.free.valid  && io.free.ready\n\n  // For the bypass case: when count==0, allocFire and freeFire happen together.\n  // The freed value goes directly out (no write to data array), count stays 0.\n  // When count>0:\n  //   allocFire: head advances, count decrements\n  //   freeFire:  write freed value to data(tail), count increments\n\n  when (bypassActive && allocFire) {\n    // Bypass: freed value goes directly to alloc output; no state change for count.\n    // If both alloc and free fire: count stays 0 (one dequeued = bypass, one enqueued = bypass consumed).\n    // Don't update head since we didn't actually read from data array.\n    // Write the freed value only if alloc didn't fire (but here alloc did fire via bypass).\n    // Net: count stays 0, head stays same.\n    // No change needed.\n  } .otherwise {\n    when (allocFire && freeFire) {\n      // Dequeue from head, enqueue at tail\n      // count stays the same (removed 1, added 1)\n      head := (head + 1.U) % capacity.U\n      data(tail) := io.free.bits\n    } .elsewhen (allocFire) {\n      head  := (head + 1.U) % capacity.U\n      count := count - 1.U\n    } .elsewhen (freeFire) {\n      data(tail) := io.free.bits\n      count      := count + 1.U\n    }\n  }\n}\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":1,"cache_creation_input_tokens":1335,"cache_read_input_tokens":63733,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":1335,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":2,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_016ja6T9yijvWsFNUiSfxi2b","session_id":"c098f578-3b36-4915-91a8-844fdc02b43c","uuid":"8e1324e1-8b0b-4943-a0d0-63b889fbc338"}

Initial pool: indices 0, 1, ..., capacity-1 (allocated sequentially via initHead pointer).\n  *  2. Free pool: a FIFO queue of returned indices (freed items are enqueued here).\n  *\n  * Allocation priority: free pool first (returned indices), then initial pool.\n  *\n  * This gives the behavior:\n  *  - Initial alloc: 0, 1, 2, 3, ...\n  *  - After freeing index i (when initial pool is exhausted): i becomes immediately available.\n  *  - \"Alloc and free on same cycle\": freed index goes to free pool front, returned before\n  *    remaining initial indices.\n  *\n  * free.ready: true when there are allocated indices outstanding (some have been allocated\n  *             but not yet freed), so accepting a freed index is meaningful.\n  *             = initHead > freePool.size  (i.e., count_allocated > 0)\n  *             = numAllocated > 0\n  *\n  * alloc.valid: true when there is an available index (free pool non-empty OR initial pool non-empty).\n  *\n  * \"No pipe\" (free.ready=false at start): initially numAllocated=0, so free.ready=false. ✓\n  * \"Flow\" (free fires immediately when all allocated): numAllocated=capacity>0, free.ready=true. ✓\n  */\nclass IndexAllocatorShifting(capacity: Int) extends IndexAllocator {\n  val indexW = log2Ceil(capacity + 1)\n\n  // Free pool: FIFO queue of freed indices. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n158\t\n159\tclass Spi2TLULV2Spec extends AnyFreeSpec with ChiselSim {\n160\t\n161\t  // Sys clock period = 10 units (SYS_HALF=5), SPI period = 13 units (SPI_HALF=6.5).\n162\t  // We use integer ratio: SYS_HALF=10, SPI_HALF=13.\n163\t  // Each clock.step(1) is one \"sim unit\". SPI toggles when the phase counter says so.\n164\t  val SYS_HALF = 10\n165\t  val SPI_HALF = 13\n166\t\n167\t  /** Run the simulation with dual-clock stepping. The main clock.step() drives the sys domain. SPI\n168\t    * clock is toggled as a Bool input at a 10:13 ratio to approximate truly async clocks.\n169\t    */\n170\t  def withDualClock(body: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper => Unit): Unit = {\n171\t    simulate(new Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) { dut =>\n172\t      // Reset — toggle SPI clock during reset so system-reset-only\n173\t      // CDC FIFOs (clocked by spi_clk) see the reset posedge.\n174\t      dut.reset.poke(true.B)\n175\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(true.B)\n176\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n177\t      dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n178\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(false.B)\n179\t      for (_ <- 0 until 5) {\n180\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(true.B)\n181\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n182\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n183\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n184\t      }\n185\t      dut.reset.poke(false.B)\n186\t      dut.clock.step(5)\n187\t\n188\t      body(dut)\n189\t    }\n190\t  }\n191\t\n192\t  /** Dual-clock tick state — tracks when to toggle SPI clock relative to sys clock. */\n193\t  class DualClockState(dut: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) {\n194\t    var sysTime: Long     = 0\n195\t    var nextSysEdge: Long = SYS_HALF\n196\t    var nextSpiEdge: Long = SPI_HALF\n197\t    var spiLevel: Boolean = false\n198\t\n199\t    /** Advance one sim time unit, toggling whichever clock(s) fire. Returns 's', 'p', or 'b'. */\n200\t    def tick(): Char = {\n201\t      if (nextSysEdge < nextSpiEdge) {\n202\t        sysTime = nextSysEdge\n203\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n204\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n205\t        's'\n206\t      } else if (nextSpiEdge < nextSysEdge) {\n207\t        sysTime = nextSpiEdge\n208\t        spiLevel = !spiLevel\n209\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n210\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n211\t        // Don't step sys clock — just toggle SPI\n212\t        // But we need at least one eval to propagate. Step sys clock to advance simulation.\n213\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n214\t        'p'\n215\t      } else {\n216\t        // Both edges coincide\n217\t        sysTime = nextSysEdge\n218\t        spiLevel = !spiLevel\n219\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n220\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n221\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n222\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n223\t        'b'\n224\t      }\n225\t    }\n226\t\n227\t    /** Advance until n SPI posedges have occurred. */\n228\t    def spiCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n229\t      var count = 0\n230\t      while (count < n) {\n231\t        val w = tick()\n232\t        if ((w == 'p' || w == 'b') && spiLevel) count += 1\n233\t      }\n234\t    }\n235\t\n236\t    /** Advance until n sys posedges have occurred. */\n237\t    def bothCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n238\t      var count = 0\n239\t      while (count < n) {\n240\t        val w = tick()\n241\t        if (w == 's' || w == 'b') count += 1\n242\t      }\n243\t    }\n244\t\n245\t    // SPI protocol helpers\n246\t\n247\t    def spiXferByte(tx: Int): Unit = {\n248\t      for (bit <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n249\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke((((tx >> bit) & 1) != 0).B)\n250\t        spiCycles(1)\n251\t      }\n252\t    }\n253\t\n254\t    def spiRecvByte(): Int = {\n255\t      var rx = 0\n256\t      for (_ <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n257\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n258\t        spiCycles(1)\n259\t        rx = (rx << 1) | (if (dut.io.spi_miso.peek().litValue != 0) 1 else 0)\n260\t      }\n261\t      rx\n262\t    }\n263\t\n264\t    def csbAssert(): Unit = {\n265\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(false.B)\n266\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n267\t    }\n268\t\n269\t    def csbDeassert(): Unit = {\n270\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n271\t      // Let DmaEngine finish draining CDC FIFOs before CSB deasserts\n272\t      // (AsyncQueue safe mode coordinates reset on CSB deassert)\n273\t      bothCycles(500)\n274\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(true.B)\n275\t      bothCycles(50)\n276\t    }\n277\t\n278\t    def spiSendHeader(op: Int, addr: Long, len: Int): Unit = {\n279\t      spiXferByte(op & 0xff)\n280\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 24) & 0xff).toInt)\n281\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 16) & 0xff).toInt)\n282\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 8) & 0xff).toInt)\n283\t      spiXferByte((addr & 0xff).toInt)\n284\t      spiXferByte((len >> 8) & 0xff)\n285\t      spiXferByte(len & 0xff)\n286\t    }\n287\t\n288\t    /** Collect n raw MISO bits. Returns array of bytes packed MSB-first per byte. */\n289\t    def collectMisoBits(nbits: Int): Array[Int] = {\n290\t      val buf = new Array[Int]((nbits + 7) / 8)\n291\t      for (i <- 0 until nbits) {\n292\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n293\t        spiCycles(1)\n294\t        val byteIdx = i / 8\n295\t        val bitIdx  = 7 - (i % 8)\n296\t        if (dut.io.spi_miso.peek().litValue != 0) {\n297\t          buf(byteIdx) |= (1 << bitIdx)\n298\t        }\n299\t      }\n300\t      buf\n301\t    }\n302\t\n303\t    /** Wait for TL-A capture count to reach expected value. */\n304\t    def waitTlACapture(expectedCount: Long, timeoutSys: Int = 200): Boolean = {\n305\t      var sc = 0\n306\t      while (sc < timeoutSys) {\n307\t        val w = tick()\n308\t        if (w == 's' || w == 'b') {\n309\t          sc += 1\n310\t          if (dut.io.tl_a_cap_count.peek().litValue >= expectedCount) return true\n311\t        }\n312\t      }\n313\t      false\n314\t    }\n315\t\n316\t    /** Reset the first-beat capture registers so the next A-channel handshake is captured. */\n317\t    def resetFirstCapture(): Unit = {\n318\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(true.B)\n319\t      dut.clock.step(1)\n320\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(false.B)\n321\t    }\n322\t\n323\t    /** Send a multi-beat write frame: header(op=0x02, addr, len=numBeats-1) + numBeats*16 payload\n324\t      * bytes.\n325\t      */\n326\t    def spiWriteMulti(addr: Long, beats: Seq[Array[Int]]): Unit = {\n327\t      csbAssert()\n328\t      spiSendHeader(0x02, addr, beats.length - 1)\n329\t      for (beat <- beats; byte <- beat) spiXferByte(byte)\n330\t      csbDeassert()\n331\t    }\n332\t\n333\t  }\n334\t\n335\t  /** Search for a bit pattern (needle) in a bit buffer (haystack). 1.U(3.W)\n75\t\n76\t  val respPending = RegInit(false.B)\n77\t  val respReq     = RegInit(0.U.asTypeOf(new OpenTitanTileLink.A_Channel(tlul_p)))\n78\t  val tlAReady    = RegInit(true.B)\n79\t\n80\t reqAddr)\n103\t\n104\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.valid       := respPending\n105\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.opcode := respOpcode.asUInt\n106\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.param  := 0.U(3.W)\n107\t  v2.io.q_tl_d.bits.size   := (latch on A-channel handshake)\n116\t  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------\n117\t  val aHandshake = aValid && tlAReady\n118\t  val captured   = RegInit(false.B)\n119\t  val capOpcode  = RegInit(0.U(3.W))\n120\t  val capAddress = RegInit(0.U(32.W))\n121\t  val capData    = RegInit(0.U(128.W))\n122\t  val capCount   = RegInit(0.U(32.W))\n123\t\n124\t  // First-beat capture: latched on the first handshake after count was last\n125\t  // snapshot by the test (i.e., the first beat of each multi-beat burst).\n126\t  val firstCapAddress = RegInit(0.U(32.W))\n127\t  val firstCapData    = RegInit(0.U(128.W))\n128\t  val firstCapDone    = RegInit(false.B)\n129\t\n130\t  captured   := Mux(aHandshake, true.B, capData)\n134\t  capCount   := Mux(aHandshake, capCount + 1.U, capCount)\n135\t\n136\t  when(io.tl_a_first_reset) {\n137\t    firstCapDone    := false.B\n138\t    firstCapAddress := 0.U\n139\t io.tl_a_cap_count     := capCount\n151\t  io.tl_a_first_address := firstCapAddress\n152\t  io.tl_a_first_data    := firstCapData\n153\t}\n154\t\n155\t// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n156\t// Test suite — ports all 6 C++ tests\n157\t// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n158\t\n159\tclass Spi2TLULV2Spec extends AnyFreeSpec with ChiselSim {\n160\t\n161\t  // Sys clock period = 10 units (SYS_HALF=5), SPI period = 13 units (SPI_HALF=6.5).\n162\t  // We use integer ratio: SYS_HALF=10, SPI_HALF=13.\n163\t  // Each clock.step(1) is one \"sim unit\". SPI toggles when the phase counter says so.\n164\t  val SYS_HALF = 10\n165\t  val SPI_HALF = 13\n166\t\n167\t  /** Run the simulation with dual-clock stepping. The main clock.step() drives the sys domain. SPI\n168\t    * clock is toggled as a Bool input at a 10:13 ratio to approximate truly async clocks.\n169\t    */\n170\t  def withDualClock(body: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper => Unit): Unit = {\n171\t    simulate(new Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) { dut =>\n172\t      // Reset — toggle SPI clock during reset so system-reset-only\n173\t      // CDC FIFOs (clocked by spi_clk) see the reset posedge.\n174\t      dut.reset.poke(true.B)\n175\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(true.B)\n176\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n177\t      dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n178\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(false.B)\n179\t      for (_ <- 0 until 5) {\n180\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(true.B)\n181\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n182\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(false.B)\n183\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n184\t      }\n185\t      dut.reset.poke(false.B)\n186\t      dut.clock.step(5)\n187\t\n188\t      body(dut)\n189\t    }\n190\t  }\n191\t\n192\t  /** Dual-clock tick state — tracks when to toggle SPI clock relative to sys clock. */\n193\t  class DualClockState(dut: Spi2TLULV2TestWrapper) {\n194\t    var sysTime: Long     = 0\n195\t    var nextSysEdge: Long = SYS_HALF\n196\t    var nextSpiEdge: Long = SPI_HALF\n197\t    var spiLevel: Boolean = false\n198\t\n199\t    /** Advance one sim time unit, toggling whichever clock(s) fire. Returns 's', 'p', or 'b'. */\n200\t    def tick(): Char = {\n201\t      if (nextSysEdge < nextSpiEdge) {\n202\t        sysTime = nextSysEdge\n203\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n204\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n205\t        's'\n206\t      } else if (nextSpiEdge < nextSysEdge) {\n207\t        sysTime = nextSpiEdge\n208\t        spiLevel = !spiLevel\n209\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n210\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n211\t        // Don't step sys clock — just toggle SPI\n212\t        // But we need at least one eval to propagate. Step sys clock to advance simulation.\n213\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n214\t        'p'\n215\t      } else {\n216\t        // Both edges coincide\n217\t        sysTime = nextSysEdge\n218\t        spiLevel = !spiLevel\n219\t        dut.io.spi_clk_in.poke(spiLevel.B)\n220\t        nextSysEdge += SYS_HALF\n221\t        nextSpiEdge += SPI_HALF\n222\t        dut.clock.step(1)\n223\t        'b'\n224\t      }\n225\t    }\n226\t\n227\t    /** Advance until n SPI posedges have occurred. */\n228\t    def spiCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n229\t      var count = 0\n230\t      while (count < n) {\n231\t        val w = tick()\n232\t        if ((w == 'p' || w == 'b') && spiLevel) count += 1\n233\t      }\n234\t    }\n235\t\n236\t    /** Advance until n sys posedges have occurred. */\n237\t    def bothCycles(n: Int): Unit = {\n238\t      var count = 0\n239\t      while (count < n) {\n240\t        val w = tick()\n241\t        if (w == 's' || w == 'b') count += 1\n242\t      }\n243\t    }\n244\t\n245\t    // SPI protocol helpers\n246\t\n247\t    def spiXferByte(tx: Int): Unit = {\n248\t      for (bit <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n249\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke((((tx >> bit) & 1) != 0).B)\n250\t        spiCycles(1)\n251\t      }\n252\t    }\n253\t\n254\t    def spiRecvByte(): Int = {\n255\t      var rx = 0\n256\t      for (_ <- 7 to 0 by -1) {\n257\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n258\t        spiCycles(1)\n259\t        rx = (rx << 1) | (if (dut.io.spi_miso.peek().litValue != 0) 1 else 0)\n260\t      }\n261\t      rx\n262\t    }\n263\t\n264\t    def csbAssert(): Unit = {\n265\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(false.B)\n266\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n267\t    }\n268\t\n269\t    def csbDeassert(): Unit = {\n270\t      dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n271\t      // Let DmaEngine finish draining CDC FIFOs before CSB deasserts\n272\t      // (AsyncQueue safe mode coordinates reset on CSB deassert)\n273\t      bothCycles(500)\n274\t      dut.io.spi_csb.poke(true.B)\n275\t      bothCycles(50)\n276\t    }\n277\t\n278\t    def spiSendHeader(op: Int, addr: Long, len: Int): Unit = {\n279\t      spiXferByte(op & 0xff)\n280\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 24) & 0xff).toInt)\n281\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 16) & 0xff).toInt)\n282\t      spiXferByte(((addr >> 8) & 0xff).toInt)\n283\t      spiXferByte((addr & 0xff).toInt)\n284\t      spiXferByte((len >> 8) & 0xff)\n285\t      spiXferByte(len & 0xff)\n286\t    }\n287\t\n288\t    /** Collect n raw MISO bits. Returns array of bytes packed MSB-first per byte. */\n289\t    def collectMisoBits(nbits: Int): Array[Int] = {\n290\t      val buf = new Array[Int]((nbits + 7) / 8)\n291\t      for (i <- 0 until nbits) {\n292\t        dut.io.spi_mosi.poke(false.B)\n293\t        spiCycles(1)\n294\t        val byteIdx = i / 8\n295\t        val bitIdx  = 7 - (i % 8)\n296\t        if (dut.io.spi_miso.peek().litValue != 0) {\n297\t          buf(byteIdx) |= (1 << bitIdx)\n298\t        }\n299\t      }\n300\t      buf\n301\t    }\n302\t\n303\t    /** Wait for TL-A capture count to reach expected value. */\n304\t    def waitTlACapture(expectedCount: Long, timeoutSys: Int = 200): Boolean = {\n305\t      var sc = 0\n306\t      while (sc < timeoutSys) {\n307\t        val w = tick()\n308\t        if (w == 's' || w == 'b') {\n309\t          sc += 1\n310\t          if (dut.io.tl_a_cap_count.peek().litValue >= expectedCount) return true\n311\t        }\n312\t      }\n313\t      false\n314\t    }\n315\t\n316\t    /** Reset the first-beat capture registers so the next A-channel handshake is captured. */\n317\t    def resetFirstCapture(): Unit = {\n318\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(true.B)\n319\t      dut.clock.step(1)\n320\t      dut.io.tl_a_first_reset.poke(false.B)\n321\t    }\n322\t\n323\t    /** Send a multi-beat write frame: header(op=0x02, addr, len=numBeats-1) + numBeats*16 payload\n324\t      * bytes.\n325\t      */\n326\t    def spiWriteMulti(addr: Long, beats: Seq[Array[Int]]): Unit = {\n327\t      csbAssert()\n328\t      spiSendHeader(0x02, addr, beats.length - 1)\n329\t      for (beat <- beats; byte <- beat) spiXferByte(byte)\n330\t      csbDeassert()\n331\t    }\n332\t\n333\t  }\n334\t\n335\t  /** Search for a bit pattern (needle) in a bit buffer (haystack). Both are packed MSB-first per\n336\t    * byte. Returns bit offset or -1.\n337\t    */\n338\t  def findBitPattern(\n339\t      haystack: Array[Int],\n340\t      hayBits: Int,\n341\t      needle: Array[Int],\n342\t      needleBits: Int\n343\t  ): Int = {\n344\t    for (off <- 0 to (hayBits - needleBits)) {\n345\t      var matched = true\n346\t      var b       = 0\n347\t      while (b < needleBits && matched) {\n348\t        val hi     = off + b\n349\t        val hayBit = (haystack(hi / 8) >> (7 - (hi % 8))) & 1\n350\t        val ndlBit = (needle(b / 8) >> (7 - (b     % 8))) & 1\n351\t        if (hayBit != ndlBit) matched = false\n352\t        b += 1\n353\t      }\n354\t      if (matched) return off\n355\t    }\n356\t    -1\n357\t  }\n358\t\n359\t  // =========================================================================\n360\t  //
